list.listitem: Use of a single dose prophylactic antibiotic in women undergoing cesarean section and vaginal preparation with povidone-iodine solution immediately before cesarean delivery reduce the incidence of endometritis.A
For women undergoing cesarean section, preoperative administration appears more effective than intraoperative antibiotics or administration at cord clamping.A

The diagnosis of post-partum endometritis is clinical using a combination of fever more than 38°C and uterine fundal tenderness occurring after the first post-delivery day in the absence of another source of infection.C

The diagnosis of chronic endometritis is usually considered for patients presenting with hypomenorrhea, secondary amenorrhea, and/or infertility and evaluation may include hysteroscopy with endometrial culture and biopsy with immunohistochemistry.C

Clindamycin and gentamicin are recommended for treatment of post-partum endometritis; once patients with uncomplicated endometritis have improved clinically (afebrile for 24-36 hours), oral therapy is not indicated.A

background.definition: Endometritis is infection or inflammation of the uterine lining; it can be acute or chronic. Postpartum endometritis is defined as inflammation of the endometrium or uterine lining following birth. Chronic endometritis is prolonged, continuous endometrial inflammation often identified during a workup for infertility.

list.listitem: In a surveillance sample of 2826 health maintenance organization (HMO) members giving birth over a 30-month period, the incidence of endometritis was 0.2% (95% CI, 0.1-0.5) for vaginal delivery among 2301 women and 0.8% (95% CI, 0.1-1.9) for cesarean delivery among 525 women, with a cesarean-section rate of 19.1%.

Authors of a Cochrane review reported an incidence of postpartum endometritis of 1% to 4% after spontaneous vaginal delivery. In a recent systematic review of high-quality studies (19% of 111 studies of infection in labor), investigators found an incidence of endometritis of 1.6% (95% CI, 0.9%-2.5%).
Of 1871 women who gave birth at a regional hospital in Denmark in a single year, nearly one quarter reported at least one or more episodes of infection including 2% with endometritis.

The incidence of postcesarean endometritis in one institution after instituting routine use of extended-spectrum prophylaxis (IV first or second generation cephalosporin plus IV azithromycin) was 6.3%; the prior rate was 19.9%.

Among 1,295 febrile peripartum women (1.6% of all parturients) in one maternity center, clinical diagnoses among infected women included endometritis (56%), chorioamnionitis ((infection of the placenta and amniotic fluid; 21%), and urosepsis (8%). Most (77%) were s/p cesarean-section and 172 (13.3%) had bacteremia. Recovered organisms included Escherichia coli (35.9%), enterococci (23.6%), anaerobic species (9.2%), and group B streptococcus (4.1%).

In a national registry study, 24 of 559 (4.3%) patients with chorioamnionitis and planned vaginal birth after cesarean section experienced postpartum infectious complications, mainly due to endometritis (19/24).
Chronic endometritis is identified in 2.8% to 57% of infertile women, 14% to 67% in women with recurrent implantation failure, and 9.3% to 68% in women with recurrent pregnancy loss.

Attributable total hospital cost of endometritis was $3,956 or $3,842 based on two different methods of cost estimates in a retrospective cohort study at a single hospital. The majority of excess costs were associated with room and board and pharmacy.
Fourth most common postpartum infection site following mastitis, urinary tract infection (UTI), and surgical site infection (eg, episiotomy, skin wound).
Chronic endometritis negatively affects embryo transfer implantation during invitro-fertilization by impairing endometrial vascularization, proper decidualization and implantation.
In a study from Denmark, more women reporting postpartum infection stopped breastfeeding within the first four weeks after delivery compared to women without infection (21% vs. 12%).
Ascending infection caused by aerobic and anaerobic bacteria.

Aerobes: Gram-positive cocci including Group B and A Streptococcus (most common), Enterococcus, other species of Streptococcus and Staphylococcus and Gram-negative cocci including Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis.
Post-cesarean section endometritis is generally due to Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus.
Recovered organisms in the case series noted above included Escherichia coli (35.9%), enterococci (23.6%), anaerobic species (9.2%), and group B streptococcus (4.1%).
In developing nations, tuberculosis is an important cause of chronic endometritis.
Anaerobes: Gram-positive cocci including Peptococcus and Peptostreptococcus species, Gram-positive bacilli including Clostridium species, Gram-negative bacilli including Bacteroides species.
Bacterial vaginosis has been associated with a higher risk of postpartum endometritis.

There are no compelling data to support length of membrane rupture, vaginal examinations, or internal monitoring as independent risk factors when controlling for length of labor. In a meta-analysis, method of cervical ripening (mechanical vs. pharmacologic) did not significantly influence postpartum endometritis rates (7.7% vs. 5.6%, respectively; pooled OR 1.35; 95% CI, 0.98-1.86).

The pathophysiology is unknown. Likely contributors are a change in the vaginal acidic environment to an alkaline 1 favoring growth of aerobic organisms and progressive necrosis of endometrial and placental remnants creating a favorable environment for multiplication of organisms.

The histopathology of acute endometritis is characterized by endometrial micro-abscesses and the presence of neutrophils in the superficial epithelium and in the lumen of the endometrial glands. In contrast, chronic endometritis is characterized by plasma cell infiltration into the endometrial stroma.
Following cesarean section, infection risk increases likely from instrumentation, the wound site, and serosanguineous fluid collection serving as a culture medium.

list.listitem: Use of a prophylactic antibiotic is recommended for women undergoing cesarean section.A
A multiple dose regimen offers no benefit over a single dose regimen (ampicillin or first-generation cephalosporin).B

Authors of a Cochrane systematic review of 95 RCTs confirmed that use of prophylactic antibiotics vs. no antibiotics in women undergoing cesarean section reduces the incidence of endometritis (RR 0.38; 95% CI, 0.34-0.42, 83 studies, 13,548 women), in addition to decreasing wound infection and maternal serious infectious complications; potential newborn effects are unclear. Similar results were seen for endometritis among women undergoing elective cesarean section (RR 0.38; 95% CI, 0.24-0.61, 15 studies).

For cesarean section prophylaxis, ampicillin or first generation cephalosporins have similar efficacy; a multiple dose regimen offers no benefit over a single dose regimen. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists guidelines (ACOG, 2018) recommend a single dose antimicrobial prophylaxis.

ACOG 2018 guidelines recommend a cephalosporin as the first-line antibiotic of choice administered within 60 minutes before the start of cesarean delivery. The addition of azithromycin, infused over 1 hour, to a standard antibiotic prophylaxis regimen may be considered for women undergoing a nonelective cesarean delivery.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 18 trials were unable to determine the optimal regimen of penicillin antibiotics for cesarean prophylaxis. They confirmed no differences between single and multiple antibiotic dose regimens (RR 1.05, 95% CI, 0.70-1.60, 5 studies) and benefit of antibiotic administration before skin incision (RR 0.21, 95% CI, 0.10–0.45, 2 studies). Combining a beta-lactamase inhibitor with a penicillin likely results in fewer cases of endometritis (RR 0.39, 95% CI, 0.21–0.72, 3 studies).

Authors of a Cochrane review found that 'antistaphylococcal cephalosporins' and 'broad spectrum penicillins plus betalactamase inhibitors' appear to have similar efficacy at caesarean section for preventing immediate postoperative infection; however, most trials administered antibiotics at or after cord clamping, or post-operatively, and current practice favors administration prior to skin incision. In addition, data are absent regarding infant outcomes or late maternal infection.

For women undergoing nonelective cesarean delivery, addition of azithromycin to routine antibiotic prophylaxis reduced rates of postpartum endometritis (3.8% vs. 6.1% without azithromycin; RR 0.62; 0.42-0.92); there were no differences in neonatal outcomes. Authors of a meta-analysis confirmed that macrolides significantly reduced the risk of endometritis (RR 0.66; 0.52 - 0.85) with no evidence of heterogeneity (I2 = 0%) based on two RCTs. Two cohort studies, including 13,809 patients, also found that azithromycin significantly reduced the risk of endometritis with a RR or 0.16; 95%, 0.04-0.62; however, significant heterogeneity was seen.

ACOG 2018 guidelines recommend consideration of vaginal cleansing before cesarean delivery in laboring patients and those with ruptured membranes using either povidone–iodine or chlorhexidine gluconate.

Vaginal preparation with povidone-iodine solution immediately before cesarean delivery reduces the risk of postoperative endometritis (3.1% in vaginal cleansing groups vs. 7.1% in control groups; a RR 0.41, 95% CI, 0.29 to 0.58, 20 trials, 6918 women, moderate-certainty evidence). The benefit of vaginal cleaning with povidone-iodine solution before cesarean delivery vs. no vaginal cleaning for reducing risk of endometritis was confirmed in a more recent network meta-analysis of 29 RCTs including 9311 women undergoing cesarean delivery (RR 0.08, 95% CI 0.01-0.69).

Authors of another meta-analysis determined that benefit of vaginal preparation was limited to women in labor before cesarean delivery (8.1% vs. 13.8%; RR 0.52, 95% CI, 0.28-0.97, 4 studies) or in those with ruptured membranes (4.3% vs. 20.1%; RR 0.23, 95% CI, 0.10-0.52; 3 studies).

In one RCT, use of chlorhexidine-alcohol single-step applicator before cesarean was comparable to povidone-iodine for antiseptic skin preparation in preventing endometritis and surgical site infections. This benefit was confirmed in the network meta-analysis noted above.

The use of vaginal chlorhexidine during labor did not prevent maternal endometritis in 3 trials. Subgroup analysis could not rule out larger reductions in endometritis with antiseptics in women who were in labor or in women with ruptured membranes.

The timing of the prophylactic dose (skin incision vs. at cord clamping) is much debated; of four recent RCTs, one found benefit in reducing endometritis giving the antibiotic at skin incision while three trials found no difference in maternal infectious or neonatal outcomes. In a large, three-arm trial of 1112 women undergoing elective cesarean section, postoperative infectious morbidity (i.e., wound infection, endometritis, or UTI) was significantly reduced with either antibiotics at skin incision or at cord clamping vs. placebo (4.9%, 3.8% and 12.1%, respectively); NNT = 13 with antibiotics vs. none.

Preoperative administration was associated with a significant reduction in the rate of endometritis compared with intraoperative administration (RR 0.59; 95% CI, 0.37-0.94; I2 0%) in a meta-analysis of six trials with 2313 women and 2345 newborns. Authors of another meta-analysis also concluded that preoperative administration reduced the risk of postpartum endometritis over administration at cord clamping (RR 0.47; 95% CI, 0.26-0.85) without increasing workups for suspected neonatal sepsis.

A systematic review of 15 studies concluded that either antibiotic administration before surgical incision or use of extended-spectrum regimens (involving azithromycin or metronidazole) after cord clamping may reduce postcesarean maternal infection by up to 50%. However, these two strategies have not been compared with each other.
Abdominal irrigation: In an RCT, abdominal irrigation at cesarean delivery increased intraoperative nausea without decreasing postoperative endometritis or other infectious morbidity.

Changing gloves during C-section: Authors of a meta-analysis of 6 studies with 1707 participants found that glove change, usually after delivery of the fetus and placenta, was associated with a reduction in the risk of incisional surgical site infection but did not reduce the risk of endometritis. This was confirmed in a meta-analysis including 7 RCTs; there was a difference in wound infective complications with a RR of 0.41 (95% CI 0.26-0.65) if glove change was performed after delivery of the placenta but no significant difference in the incidence of endometritis.

Two randomized trials found use of antibiotics for prelabor rupture of membranes (PROM) at term reduced maternal chorioamnionitis or endometritis (RR 0.4; 95% CI, 0.2-0.8; NNT 25) but the authors caution that addition study is warranted.

Based on 9 RCTs including 3759 patients with singleton cephalic gestations and prelabor rupture of membranes at ≥36 weeks, induction of labor ≤12 hours after membrane rupture was associated with significantly fewer incidences of chorioamnionitis (5.3% vs 9.9%; RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.40-0.97), endometritis (2.4% vs 4.2%; RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.40-0.87), neonatal sepsis (6.1% vs 11.8%; RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.27-0.79), and admission to neonatal intensive care unit (6.4% vs 12.0%; RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.43-0.69) compared with women managed expectantly.

Authors of a Cochrane review concluded that there was no convincing evidence of benefit for mothers or neonates from the routine use of antibiotics for PROM at or near term. This conclusion was based on four studies demonstrating no differences in primary outcomes including neonatal sepsis and maternal infectious morbidity.

Speculum examination only vs. digital examination in women with preterm prelabor rupture of membranes was associated with less maternal infectious morbidity, defined as chorioamnionitis, endometritis or both (26% vs. 33%, pooled OR 0.75, 95% CI 0.58-0.98, I2 17%) based on 4 cohort studies including 1213 women.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 2 RCTs (one large) found benefit of a single-dose antibiotic at delivery to prevent superficial and deep perineal wound infection for women undergoing operative (vacuum and forceps-assisted) vaginal deliveries, but data were unclear on benefit for endometritis.
Authors of a Cochrane review, based on a single trial, found no benefit of prophylactic antibiotics on prevention of postpartum endometritis among women with meconium-stained amniotic fluid.

Antibiotics after vaginal delivery for women with ragged placental membranes did not result in a reduction of endometritis (0.90% vs. 0.29% without prophylaxis); based on an RCT of 716 women (10.9% of vaginal deliveries at the 3 institutions).

Evidence is very uncertain regarding the benefit of prophylactic antibiotics for preventing postpartum endometritis following manual removal of the placenta. This was based on 4 studies with 974 participants and a RR of 0.94 (95% CI 0.48 to 1.85).
The diagnosis is clinical using a combination of fever more than 38°C and uterine fundal tenderness occurring after the first post-delivery day in the absence of another source of infection.C

Patients with chronic endometriosis may have ill-defined symptoms of pelvic discomfort, spotting and leucorrhea or concerns with hypomenorrhea, secondary amenorrhea, and/or infertility.C Testing used in diagnosis is discussed below.

Breast pain, erythema, skin change (woody feel, abscess)
Pain at wound site, erythema, purulent discharge
Fails to improve with antibiotic therapy or occurring 7-10 days after delivery

list.listitem: Endometritis should be suspected if a woman develops fever in the postpartum period or following instrumentation.
The diagnosis is clinical with a combination of fever more than 38°C and uterine fundal tenderness occurring after the first post-delivery day in the absence of another source of infection.
Foul smelling lochia may be seen but this finding is inconsistent.
Patients with chronic endometritis can have no symptoms or ill-defined symptoms of pelvic discomfort, spotting and leucorrhea or present with hypomenorrhea, secondary amenorrhea, and/or infertility.

Physical examination should include the lungs (pneumonia, atelectasis), breasts (breast engorgement, mastitis), abdomen (pain localization), and perineum (local infection); the incision should be inspected in women post cesarean section.
There are no specific laboratory tests for endometritis; cultures (genital and blood) are rarely useful.
A post-delivery leukocyte count, in 1 study, did not predict postpartum infection in women undergoing cesarean delivery.
Urine culture should be obtained to rule out UTI.

Ultrasound may assist in the diagnosis of endometritis in postpartum patients with abdominal pain and fever; findings of endometritis are a thickened, heterogeneous endometrium, fluid collection in the uterus, and foci of air in the uterus. However, these ultrasound findings may also be seen in normal postpartum patients and patients with endometritis may have a normal pelvic ultrasound.

In cases of suspected subclinical or chronic endometritis, hysteroscopy with endometrial culture and biopsy can be considered for diagnosis. The dominant hysteroscopic features are micropolyposis, stromal edema or congestion, and diffuse or focal hyperemia.

Endometrial plasma cells can sometimes be identified, and immunohistochemistry for CD138, a transmembrane heparin sulphate proteoglycan and a plasma cell marker, is considered a reliable diagnostic marker despite lack of standardization.
Suspect endometritis in women who are postpartum or have had recent instrumentation and present with fever and/or uterine fundal tenderness.
Genital and blood cultures are rarely helpful; order urine culture to rule out UTI.
Clindamycin (900 mg IV every 8 hours) and gentamicin (1.5 mg/kg every 8 hours) are recommended for treatment of post-partum endometritis.A
Once patients with uncomplicated endometritis have improved clinically (afebrile for 24-36 hours), oral therapy is not indicated.A

Clindamycin (900 mg IV every 8 hours) and gentamicin (1.5 mg/kg every 8 hours) are recommended for treatment; once patients with uncomplicated endometritis have improved clinically (afebrile for 24-36 hours), oral therapy is not indicated.

Because of potential complications of diarrhea (clindamycin) and oto and renal toxicity (gentamicin), other single agent antibiotics have been tested including single agent cefamandole, cefoxitin, cefotaxime, and piperacillin; in the 15 trials identified in a Cochrane review where an alternative agent(s) was tested against clindamycin and an aminoglycoside, there were more treatment failures with the alternative regimen (RR 1.44; 95% CI, 1.15-1.8). There were more treatment failures (RR 1.94, 95% CI, 1.38 to 2.72; 774 participants; 7 studies) in those treated with a regimen with poor activity against penicillin‐resistant anaerobic bacteria compared to those treated with a regimen with good activity against penicillin‐resistant anaerobic bacteria.
Single daily dosing (2700 mg clindamycin and 5 mg/kg gentamicin) in 1 small study was at least equally effective.

CDC 2021 guidelines for sexually-transmitted infections recommend the following parenteral regimens for pelvic inflammatory disease: ceftriaxone 1 g every 24 hours PLUS doxycycline 100 mg orally or IV every 12 hours PLUS metronidazole 500 my orally or IV every 12 hours. Alternatively, they recommend either cefotetan 2 g every 12 hours PLUS doxycycline 100 mg orally or IV every 12 hours or cefoxitin 2 g every 6 hours PLUS doxycycline 100 mg orally or IV every 12 hours.
Antibiotic regimens include doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days OR ciprofloxacin and metronidazole 500 mg daily for two weeks OR ofloxacin 400 mg and metronidazole 500 mg daily for two weeks.

Authors of a meta-analysis including 33 RCTs of women with endometritis found that women randomized to use of the traditional Chinese medicine Fuke Qianjin in addition to conventional treatment had higher clinical effectiveness (OR for cure 5.1, 95% CI, 4.0-6.4) and improved secondary endpoints such as normalization of menses, irregular vaginal bleeding and relapse rate with no significant publication bias or small sample effect. There was no significant difference between groups in adverse events.
A rapid response is seen in over 90% of women following antibiotic treatment.B
Streptococcal Toxic Shock Syndrome is a rare but serious condition of streptococcal postpartum endometritis.C

Chronic endometritis, as noted in prevalence, is associated with impaired fertility.A Authors of a meta-analysis of 9 studies of patients with recurrent implantation failure concluded that antibiotic treatment may improve pregnancy outcomes in subsequent IVF cycles but only in patients with confirmed chronic endometritis.
